_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Mongolia covering Xiongnu confederation, Turks/Uyghur khaganates, Khitan Liao, Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire (1206, largest contiguous empire), Yuan Dynasty, Northern Yuan, Manchu Qing conquest, Bogd Khanate (1911 independence), Outer Mongolia autonomy, Soviet-backed Mongolian People's Republic (1924, second communist state), 1990 democratic revolution, market economy transition, mining boom, and balancing China-Russia via 'third neighbour' policy.

religion.note: Tibetan Buddhism suppressed under communism; revival post-1990; Gandantegchinlen Monastery; Dalai Lama ties; Kazakhs are Muslim; shamanic/Tengriist traditions persist; communist era left large non-religious population

ethnic_groups.name: Khalkha Mongol
ethnic_groups.notes: Dominant group; standard Mongolian based on Khalkha dialect; nomadic pastoralist traditions (though urbanising); Cyrillic script since 1941; politically dominant

ethnic_groups.name: Kazakh
ethnic_groups.notes: Bayan-Ölgii province; Muslim; Turkic language; eagle hunting; autonomous cultural region; some emigration to Kazakhstan

ethnic_groups.name: Dorvod
ethnic_groups.notes: Oirat subgroup; western Mongolia; distinct dialect

ethnic_groups.name: Buryat
ethnic_groups.notes: Northern Mongolia; cross-border with Russia (Buryatia); Buddhist; some Russian cultural influence

ethnic_groups.name: Zakhchin, Dariganga, Uriankhai, other Mongolic
ethnic_groups.notes: Various Mongol tribes; Oirat and Khalkha subgroups; reindeer-herding Tsaatan (Dukha) in far north

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese, Russian, Tuvan, Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Small Chinese and Russian minorities; Tuvan in far west; communist-era Russians mostly left

independence.from: Qing China (1911), then Mongolia People's Republic declared 1924; independence recognised by China only 1945

country_profile.notes_unique: World's most sparsely populated sovereign country (~2 people/km²); landlocked between China and Russia; Genghis Khan legacy central to national identity; Oyu Tolgoi (massive copper/gold mine); nomadic pastoralism (~30% nomadic); coldest capital city globally; Gobi Desert; wild horses (Przewalski); throat singing (khöömei); 'third neighbour' policy balances China-Russia via US/Japan/EU ties

current_leader.name: Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: Mongolian People's Party (MPP); former PM; presidential powers limited in semi-presidential system

prime_minister.name: Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene
prime_minister.title: Prime Minister
prime_minister.notes: MPP (successor to communist-era MPRP); economist; youngest PM in Mongolia's democratic history

former_leaders.name: Khaltmaagiin Battulga
former_leaders.notes: Democratic Party; businessman; wrestler; nationalist; tensions with MPP parliament; lost re-election

former_leaders.name: Tsakhiagiin Elbegdorj
former_leaders.notes: Democratic Party; two terms; journalist activist in 1990 revolution; anti-corruption; abolished death penalty

former_leaders.name: Nambaryn Enkhbayar
former_leaders.notes: MPRP; later convicted of corruption; established Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party (split)

former_leaders.name: Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat
former_leaders.notes: First post-communist president; initially MPRP then independent; 1990 democratic revolution leader; peaceful transition

910.name: Xiongnu Empire
910.description: The first great nomadic empire of the Mongolian steppe, the Xiongnu confederation that rivaled Han China, built the template for steppe empires, and may be ancestral to the European Huns.

sub_clusters.name: Modu Chanyu and Xiongnu Rise
sub_clusters.description: Modu Chanyu's unification of the steppe peoples, the humiliating defeat of Han Emperor Gaozu at Baideng, the heqin tribute system, and the vast Xiongnu confederation from Manchuria to Central Asia.
key_events: Modu Chanyu unifies the steppe and defeats Han Emperor Gaozu at Baideng (200 BC)
Han dynasty begins heqin policy — sending princesses and tribute to the Xiongnu

sub_clusters.name: Han-Xiongnu Wars and Decline
sub_clusters.description: Emperor Wu's aggressive campaigns against the Xiongnu, the split into Northern and Southern Xiongnu, the southern submission to Han, and the northern Xiongnu's westward migration.
key_events: Emperor Wu launches major campaigns against the Xiongnu (133 BC onwards)
Northern Xiongnu defeated and driven westward — possible ancestors of the Huns (89–93 AD)

910.name: Rouran and Turkic Khaganates
910.description: The succession of steppe empires after the Xiongnu: the Rouran (Avars), the first and second Turkic Khaganates, and their roles in Eurasian trade and power dynamics.

sub_clusters.name: Rouran Khaganate
sub_clusters.description: The Rouran confederation's dominance of the Mongolian steppe, their invention of the title 'khagan,' relations with Chinese northern dynasties, and their overthrow by the Göktürks.

sub_clusters.name: Turkic Khaganates
sub_clusters.description: The First and Second Turkic Khaganates spanning from Manchuria to the Byzantine frontier, the Orkhon inscriptions as the oldest Turkic writing, and the Göktürk legacy in Mongolian steppe culture.
key_events: Bilge Khagan's Orkhon inscriptions — oldest known Turkic script monuments (732–735 AD)

910.name: Uyghur and Khitan Empires
910.description: The Uyghur Khaganate's adoption of Manichaeism and urban culture, followed by the Khitan Liao dynasty's dual administration system bridging nomadic and sedentary worlds.

sub_clusters.name: Uyghur Khaganate
sub_clusters.description: The Uyghur Khaganate as a key ally of Tang China during the An Lushan Rebellion, the unique adoption of Manichaeism as state religion, urban construction at Ordu-Baliq, and the Kirghiz destruction.
key_events: Uyghurs help Tang China suppress the An Lushan Rebellion (756–757)

sub_clusters.name: Khitan Liao Dynasty
sub_clusters.description: The Khitan creation of the Liao dynasty ruling northern China and the steppe, the innovative dual administration system for nomadic and sedentary subjects, and the Khitan script.
key_events: Abaoji founds the Khitan Liao dynasty with a dual northern-southern administration (907)

920.name: Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan
920.description: The rise of Temüjin from orphaned outcast to Genghis Khan, the creation of the largest contiguous land empire in history, the Mongol military revolution, and the Yasa legal code.

sub_clusters.name: Rise of Genghis Khan
sub_clusters.description: Temüjin's early hardships, his alliances and rivalries on the steppe, the unification of the Mongol tribes, and his proclamation as Genghis Khan at the great kurultai.
key_events: Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan ('Universal Ruler') at the kurultai (1206)

sub_clusters.name: Mongol Conquests
sub_clusters.description: The destruction of the Khwarezmian Empire, the conquest of northern China, the campaigns in Russia and Eastern Europe, and the world empire spanning from Korea to Hungary under Genghis Khan's successors.
key_events: Genghis Khan destroys the Khwarezmian Empire — Bukhara, Samarkand, and Merv devastated (1219–1221)
Mongol forces reach the gates of Vienna before withdrawing after Ögedei Khan's death (1241–1242)

920.name: Successor Khanates and Yuan Connection
920.description: The fragmentation of the empire into the Golden Horde, Chagatai, Ilkhanate, and Yuan dynasty, the Pax Mongolica facilitating Silk Road trade, and the gradual decline of Mongol political unity.

sub_clusters.name: Kublai Khan and Mongol China
sub_clusters.description: Kublai Khan's establishment of the Yuan dynasty in China, his rivalry with Kaidu in Central Asia, the failed invasions of Japan and Java, and the integration of Mongolia into a China-centered empire.
key_events: Kublai Khan moves the capital to Dadu (Beijing) and proclaims the Yuan dynasty (1271)

sub_clusters.name: Pax Mongolica and Decline
sub_clusters.description: The unprecedented Eurasian connectivity of the Pax Mongolica, Marco Polo and other travelers, the spread of the Black Death along trade routes, and the expulsion of the Mongols from China.
key_events: Marco Polo travels through the Mongol Empire to Kublai Khan's court (1271–1295)
Red Turban Rebellion expels the Mongols from China — Yuan dynasty falls (1368)

930.name: Northern Yuan and Post-Imperial Mongolia
930.description: The retreat to the steppe after losing China, the Northern Yuan successor state, the Oirat-Eastern Mongol rivalry, and the brief reunification under Dayan Khan and Altan Khan.

sub_clusters.name: Northern Yuan and Fragmentation
sub_clusters.description: The continuation of Mongol imperial claims as the Northern Yuan, the civil wars between Borjigin princes, the rise of the Oirat confederation, and Esen Taishi's capture of the Ming emperor.
key_events: Esen Taishi captures Ming Emperor Yingzong at the Battle of Tumu (1449)

sub_clusters.name: Dayan Khan and Altan Khan
sub_clusters.description: Dayan Khan's reunification of the Eastern Mongols, Altan Khan's alliance with Tibetan Buddhism and the bestowal of the Dalai Lama title, and the conversion of Mongolia to Tibetan Buddhism.
key_events: Altan Khan bestows the title 'Dalai Lama' on Sonam Gyatso — Mongolia converts to Buddhism (1578)

930.name: Mongolia under Qing Rule
930.description: The Manchu conquest of Inner and Outer Mongolia, the Qing administrative system of leagues and banners, the Dzungar genocide, the spread of monastic Buddhism, and growing Chinese colonization.

sub_clusters.name: Manchu Conquest and Dzungar Wars
sub_clusters.description: The submission of Inner Mongolia to the Manchus, the Khalkha Mongols' submission after Dzungar attacks, the Qing campaigns that annihilated the Dzungar Khanate, and the banner system administration.
key_events: Khalkha Mongols submit to the Qing to escape Dzungar aggression (1691)
Qing annihilation of the Dzungar Khanate — estimated 80% of the Dzungar population killed (1755–1759)

sub_clusters.name: Qing-Era Monasticism and Decline
sub_clusters.description: The proliferation of Buddhist monasteries with up to 40% of males becoming monks, the role of the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu as spiritual leader, economic stagnation, Chinese colonization, and growing national consciousness.

940.name: Bogd Khanate and Independence
940.description: Mongolia's declaration of independence during the Xinhai Revolution, the theocratic Bogd Khanate, the Chinese reoccupation, Baron Ungern-Sternberg's brief mad rule, and the Soviet-backed revolution.

sub_clusters.name: Declaration of Independence
sub_clusters.description: The Bogd Khan's declaration of independence from the Qing, the theocratic government, Russian protection, and the Chinese military reoccupation under Xu Shuzheng that ended autonomy.
key_events: Outer Mongolia declares independence with the 8th Jebtsundamba Khutuktu as Bogd Khan (1911)

sub_clusters.name: Ungern-Sternberg and Revolution of 1921
sub_clusters.description: Baron Ungern-Sternberg's White Russian capture of Urga, the Mongolian People's Party's alliance with Soviet Russia, Sükhbaatar's liberation of the capital, and the founding of the People's Republic.
key_events: Sükhbaatar and Soviet forces liberate Urga from Ungern-Sternberg (1921)
Mongolian People's Republic proclaimed after the Bogd Khan's death (1924)

950.name: Mongolian People's Republic
950.description: Mongolia as a Soviet satellite state for nearly seven decades, Choibalsan's Stalinist purges, the destruction of monasteries, collectivization, the Sino-Soviet border tensions, and gradual modernization.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinist Era and Purges
sub_clusters.description: The consolidation of communist rule, Choibalsan's Great Purge destroying the Buddhist establishment with over 700 monasteries and 17,000 monks killed, forced collectivization, and Mongolian participation in the Battle of Khalkhin Gol.
key_events: Choibalsan's purges destroy Mongolia's Buddhist establishment — over 700 monasteries demolished (1937–1939)
Battle of Khalkhin Gol — Soviet-Mongolian forces defeat Japan (1939)

sub_clusters.name: Cold War Mongolia
sub_clusters.description: Tsedenbal's long rule, Soviet economic aid and military bases, the Sino-Soviet split placing Mongolia between two hostile powers, UN membership, and tentative modernization of the pastoral economy.
key_events: Mongolia admitted to the United Nations (1961)

960.name: Democratic Revolution and Modern Mongolia
960.description: Mongolia's peaceful democratic revolution, the transition to a market economy, the mining boom, the revival of Genghis Khan as a national symbol, and the challenges of democracy on the steppe.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Revolution of 1990
sub_clusters.description: The peaceful pro-democracy protests in Sükhbaatar Square, the adoption of a new democratic constitution, the painful economic transition from communism, and the revival of Buddhism and traditional culture.
key_events: Peaceful democratic revolution — Mongolia adopts a new constitution (1990–1992)

sub_clusters.name: Mining Boom and Contemporary Challenges
sub_clusters.description: The Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine and resource nationalism debates, rapid urbanization with nearly half the population in Ulaanbaatar, air pollution crises, the 'third neighbor' foreign policy, and pastoral nomadism's uncertain future.
key_events: Oyu Tolgoi agreement signed — one of the world's largest copper-gold mines (2009)
Mongolia hosts the first-ever papal visit to the country by Pope Francis (2023)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
